title: Session fixation and password storage
summary: Rotate the session at sign-in so a planted id is worthless, end sessions on the server, and store passwords so a database dump does not become a list of passwords: salted, slow, and compared in constant time.

steps.title: Session fixation: the attacker picks your session id
body: 1. attacker   GET /             -> Set-Cookie: sid=A77   (an anonymous session)
2. attacker   plants sid=A77 in the victim's browser (a link on a sibling subdomain, a shared computer)
3. victim     POST /login        -> 302 /   the server marks session A77 as "carol" and keeps the id
4. attacker   GET /account  Cookie: sid=A77   -> carol's account

The bug is step 3: signing in **upgraded** an existing session instead of issuing a new one. The rule: **issue a fresh, random session id whenever privilege changes**: at sign-in, at sign-out, after MFA, after a password change. ASP.NET Core's cookie authentication does this for you (`SignInAsync` writes a new ticket); hand-written session tables must do it themselves.

Also end sessions **on the server**. Deleting the cookie in the browser at sign-out does nothing if the old id still works when replayed. After a password change or an incident, revoke every session of that user.

steps.prompt: Which sign-in code is safe against session fixation?
options: Delete the old session row, create a new random id, and set it as the cookie
Keep the session id, set session.UserId = carol
Keep the session id but make the cookie HttpOnly
Keep the session id and add the user's IP address to it
steps.explain: HttpOnly stops scripts reading the id, not an attacker who already knows it. Binding to an IP breaks mobile users and does not stop an attacker on the same network.

steps.title: Storing passwords: what a dump should give an attacker
body: The lab's shop stores `sha256(password)`. From a SQL injection dump, an attacker cracks every common password in seconds: SHA-256 runs billions of times a second on a GPU, and with no salt one precomputed table covers every user.
| plain text, reversible encryption, MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 (salted or not) | broken for passwords: too fast |
| **Argon2id** (m=19 MiB, t=2, p=1 or stronger) | OWASP's first choice; a NuGet package in .NET |
| ASP.NET Core Identity `PasswordHasher` | PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512, 100,000 iterations, random salt; fine, and it upgrades old hashes on sign-in |

Three rules whatever the algorithm: a **random salt per password** (16 bytes from `RandomNumberGenerator`), the **algorithm and cost stored with the hash** (so you can raise them later), and **constant-time comparison** (`CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`).

items: PBKDF2 with a fixed salt for every user
steps.explain: Encryption is reversible: whoever gets the key gets every password. A fixed salt lets one precomputed table attack all users again.

code: var a = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2("sunshine1", new byte[16], 1000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32);
var b = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2("sunshine1", new byte[16], 1000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32);
steps.explain: Same password and salt, same hash: that is how verifying works. A different salt gives a completely different hash, which is why each user gets their own random one.

steps.title: Hash and verify, the stored-format way
prompt: - `string HashPassword(string password)` returns `pbkdf2-sha256$600000$<salt>$<hash>`: a fresh 16-byte random salt, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations, a 32-byte hash, salt and hash in Base64;

- `bool VerifyPassword(string password, string stored)` parses that format, recomputes with the **stored** iteration count and salt, and compares with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`. Anything that is not in the format (an old unsalted hex hash, a missing part, bad Base64, iterations that are not a positive number) returns `false`, never throws.
starter: bool VerifyPassword(string password, string stored) => HashPassword(password) == stored;
solution: if (parts.Length != 4 || parts[0] != "pbkdf2-sha256" || !int.TryParse(parts[1], out var iterations) || iterations < 1) return false;
var actual = Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, iterations, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, expected.Length);
hints: `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16)` for the salt, `Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2(password, salt, 600_000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32)` for the hash.
In `VerifyPassword`, `stored.Split('$')` must give 4 parts with the right prefix; decode inside a `try` that catches `FormatException`.
template: var h1 = HashPassword("correct horse battery staple");
var h2 = HashPassword("correct horse battery staple");
Dojo.Check("the format is pbkdf2-sha256$600000$salt$hash", p.Length == 4 && p[0] == "pbkdf2-sha256" && p[1] == "600000", h1);
Dojo.Eq("the salt is 16 bytes", 16, p.Length == 4 ? Convert.FromBase64String(p[2]).Length : 0);
Dojo.Eq("the hash is 32 bytes", 32, p.Length == 4 ? Convert.FromBase64String(p[3]).Length : 0);
Dojo.Check("the same password hashes differently each time (random salt)", h1 != h2, h1);
Dojo.Eq("the right password verifies", true, VerifyPassword("correct horse battery staple", h1));
Dojo.Eq("a wrong password does not", false, VerifyPassword("Correct horse battery staple", h1));
var dojoQuick = "pbkdf2-sha256$1000$" + Convert.ToBase64String(new byte[16]) + "$" + Convert.ToBase64String(Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2("sunshine1", new byte[16], 1000, HashAlgorithmName.SHA256, 32));
Dojo.Eq("the stored iteration count is used", true, VerifyPassword("sunshine1", dojoQuick));
Dojo.Eq("an old unsalted SHA-256 hex hash is not accepted", false, VerifyPassword("sunshine1", Convert.ToHexStringLower(SHA256.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("sunshine1")))));
Dojo.Eq("bad Base64 returns false", false, VerifyPassword("x", "pbkdf2-sha256$1000$!!!$!!!"));
Dojo.Eq("zero iterations returns false", false, VerifyPassword("x", "pbkdf2-sha256$0$AAAA$AAAA"));
Dojo.Eq("an empty string returns false", false, VerifyPassword("x", ""));
